# Hierarchical, Graph-Based, and Adaptive Structures

Also called: Adaptive Spatial Partitioning, Elastic Inference, Gaussian Mixture Tree, Mipmap-GS, Hierarchical Anchor Coupling, Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids, Surface-Aware Splat Graph, KoalaGS, Hierarchical 3D Gaussian BVH Construction

## Overview
This family of methods extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing structured data representations (graphs, trees, grids) and adaptive mechanisms to handle large-scale scenes, varying computational budgets, and geometric fidelity. While standard 3DGS treats primitives as an unstructured flat list, these methods organize Gaussians to enable efficient culling, compression, deformation, or multi-scale rendering. They solve problems such as memory overflow in large scenes, aliasing at extreme zoom levels, and the inability to adapt model size to hardware constraints without retraining.

## Shared principles
The methods in this family share the goal of modifying the standard flat Gaussian representation to improve scalability, adaptability, or geometric consistency. Common mechanisms include:
1.  **Structural Organization:** Grouping Gaussians into hierarchical trees (e.g., octrees, BVHs, Gaussian Mixture Trees) or graphs (camera connectivity, surface adjacency) to enable spatial or semantic queries.
2.  **Adaptive Selection/Transformation:** Dynamically selecting a subset of Gaussians or transforming their attributes (position, scale, color) based on external constraints (e.g., target ratio, zoom level) or internal metrics (e.g., reconstruction loss, geometric similarity).
3.  **Cross-Level/Neighbor Interaction:** Propagating information between related primitives (e.g., parent-child in a tree, neighbors in a graph) to enforce consistency, regularization, or feature enhancement.

## Subtopics

### [TraGraph-GS](14454-tragraph-gs.md)
TraGraph-GS is a rendering method for arbitrary large-scale scenes that uses graph-based adaptive spatial partitioning, regularization constraints for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), and adaptive region selection to handle vast scales while maintaining real-time performance. It differs from standard 3DGS by explicitly modeling camera connectivity to partition the scene into balanced, connected subgraphs, and from other hierarchical methods by using a progressive blending strategy of local and global Gaussian representations to eliminate boundary artifacts.

### [FlexGS](16110-flexgs.md)
FlexGS is an elastic inference method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables a single trained model to adapt to varying computational constraints at inference time by selecting and transforming a subset of Gaussians based on a desired model size ratio, without requiring additional fine-tuning. It solves the problem that standard 3DGS models are too memory-intensive for devices with restricted resources (e.g., smartphones, VR headsets) and that previous compression methods require costly retraining or separate model generation for each target hardware configuration. Unlike post-hoc compression methods that use fixed heuristics to retain Top-K Gaussians and require separate runs for each ratio, FlexGS jointly trains a learnable module to adaptively select points based on attributes and the desired ratio during training.

### [Gaussian Mixture Tree Construction](16717-gaussian-mixture-tree-construction.md)
Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT) Construction is a hierarchical scene representation method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a tree structure to identify distinct 3D plane instances. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which treats primitives as independent entities, GMT recursively merges leaf nodes (local clusters of Gaussians) into parent nodes based on statistical similarity and geometric consistency, enabling plane-aware rendering and deformation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [TraGraph-GS](14454-tragraph-gs.md) and [Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction](22007-surface-aware-splat-graph-construction.md) by its explicit tree hierarchy derived from Gaussian Mixture Models rather than graph adjacency or spatial containment.

### [Mipmap-GS](16893-mipmap-gs.md)
Mipmap-GS is a test-time adaptation method that deforms pre-trained 3D Gaussian primitives to resolve aliasing artifacts (zoom-in spikes and zoom-out thickness) caused by fixed Gaussian distributions at varying zoom factors. Unlike sibling methods that apply post-processing filters or hierarchical level-of-detail selection, Mipmap-GS self-adjusts primitive properties (color, shape, size) and distribution (position) by optimizing against scale-specific mipmap-like pseudo ground-truth, effectively informing the Gaussians of the new sampling rate.

### [Hierarchical Anchor Coupling](17260-hierarchical-anchor-coupling.md)
Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) is a module that establishes cross-level gradient pathways in structured 3D Gaussian splatting by aggregating context from adjacent octree levels and broadcasting a residual feature adjustment to visible anchors. It solves the problem of feature isolation, where backpropagation graphs in anchor-based octrees lack connections between features at level $l_i$ and their neighbors at $l_i \pm 1$. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial lookup or graph edges, HAC operates at the octree level granularity, providing a shared regularization signal that improves performance on dense, repetitive structures while adding negligible parameters.

### [Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids](19022-self-organizing-gaussian-grids.md)
Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids is a compact 3D scene representation that organizes the high-dimensional parameters of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into a 2D grid with local homogeneity to drastically reduce storage size without compromising visual quality. It exploits perceptual redundancies in natural scenes, where numerous permutations of Gaussian parameters can equivalently represent the same scene, by mapping these parameters into a 2D layout that preserves topological relationships through competitive learning. Unlike fixed-ordering methods such as Z-order curves or tri-planes, this representation is learned per scene, allowing neighbors in all dimensions to be modeled effectively.

### [Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction](22007-surface-aware-splat-graph-construction.md)
Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction establishes connectivity between 3D Gaussian primitives exclusively along the underlying surface manifold, filtering out spurious neighbors that are close in Euclidean space but distant along the surface. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which relies on rasterization order or Euclidean distance for neighbor queries, this method defines edges based on the geometric intersection of Gaussian kernels. It is chosen when faithful surface topology preservation is required for downstream tasks such as Laplacian-based deformation, where Euclidean kNN would introduce topological errors.

#### KoalaGS
**Definition:** A deformation technique that builds a Laplacian operator directly on the collection of Gaussian kernel means $\{\pi_i\}_{i=1}^N$, treating them as a point cloud, using geodesic distance on the splat graph to reflect the underlying surface faithfully [S1].
**Steps:**
1. Construct the Laplacian operator $\Delta$ on the set of Gaussian kernel means $\{\pi_i\}_{i=1}^N$. Integrate the surface-aware splat graph into off-the-shelf point cloud Laplacian methods [S1].
2. Use graph geodesic distance rather than raw graph connectivity for robustness against missing edges. Compute the cotangent Laplacian on a local triangulation using NonManifold [S1].
3. Deform the means of kernels $\{\pi_i\}_{i=1}^N$ through a Laplacian-based deformation map $\phi_\Delta$ obtained by solving a system such as ARAP [1] or BBW [2] using the Laplacian operator $\Delta$ [S1].
**Pitfall:** Simply displacing the positions of the primitives leads to severe visual artifacts because the covariances of the Gaussian kernels are not adapted properly [S1].

#### Hierarchical 3D Gaussian BVH Construction
**Definition:** The resulting BVH tree ensures that the children of each interior node will be spatially compact [S2].
**Steps:**
1. Initialize the root node of the BVH as the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of all Gaussians, using 3x their stored size to capture extent [S2].
2. Recursively perform a binary median split on the current node to obtain child nodes [S2].
3. Project the means of all Gaussians in the group onto the longest axis of their bounding box [S2].
4. Partition the group by assigning each primitive based on the position of its projected mean with respect to the median of all projections [S2].
5. Compute intermediate node Gaussians from their respective children, starting from the leaves and recursively merging up the tree [S2].

## Background
The need for hierarchical and adaptive structures in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the limitations of the original flat representation, particularly regarding scalability to large scenes, memory efficiency on edge devices, and geometric consistency for deformation. Standard 3DGS [Kerbl et al. 2023] stores all Gaussians in a flat list, which becomes inefficient for scenes with millions of primitives or when rendering at varying resolutions.

TraGraph-GS addresses large-scale scene rendering by partitioning the scene based on camera connectivity, ensuring that local regions are coherent and can be rendered independently [S1]. FlexGS tackles the inference-time adaptability problem, allowing a single model to serve different hardware constraints by dynamically selecting and transforming Gaussians [S1]. Gaussian Mixture Tree Construction introduces a hierarchical structure based on statistical similarity to identify planar surfaces, aiding in deformation and rendering [S1]. Mipmap-GS addresses aliasing artifacts at extreme zoom levels by adapting Gaussian properties to the sampling rate [S1]. Hierarchical Anchor Coupling improves feature consistency in octree-based representations by linking adjacent levels [S1]. Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids reduce storage size by organizing parameters into a 2D grid [S2]. Surface-Aware Splat Graph Construction ensures that graph-based operations (like Laplacian deformation) respect the underlying surface topology rather than Euclidean proximity [S1].

The concept of hierarchical BVH construction for 3D Gaussians is also explored to optimize spatial queries and culling, ensuring spatial compactness of nodes [S2]. These methods collectively represent a shift from static, unstructured Gaussian representations to dynamic, structured, and adaptive ones.
